Cullet containing antimony oxide cannot be used in float glass production, but it can be used in rolled glass production. • Low-iron silica sand: See Section 2.8.5. • FTO: FTO is applied to manufactured float glass using chemical vapor deposition with fluorine and tin gases. United States primarily sourced from Mexico in 2024 (U.S. Geological Survey 2025g). Tin sourcing is described below. For FTO coatings, tin is introduced to the chamber in a chloride gas or organo-metallic gas form (Allendorf et al. 2006). • Tin bath: Float glass is produced by pouring molten glass onto a tin bath kept molten with electricity, ensuring a smooth surface. The tin bath can be 3–8 m wide, 50–60 m long, and 6 cm deep (Leftheriotis and Yianoulis 2012), implying 63–200 t of tin per float line. The tin bath must be kept in a reducing environment of nitrogen and hydrogen (3%– 10%), and it is possible to implement a gas recovery and reuse system (Greg Morris 2015). Tin consumption for float glass baths constitutes less than 26% of total domestic demand. We estimate the tin bath does not require frequent replacement. There is no U.S. mining or smelting of tin. Refined tin imports to the United States come primarily from Peru, Bolivia, Indonesia, and Brazil (U.S. Geological Survey 2025a). • Equipment: Equipment is readily available from several vendors, and new lines or upgrades can be implemented in less than 2 years (USGlass Magazine 2023c). Float line capacity can range from 50 to 1,200 t/day (Stewart Engineers 2024). 66 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 4 Structural Components 4.1 Overview This section covers supply chains for the structural elements used in PV systems. See Appendix B for information on raw materials used in many structural products. The United States hosts a growing base of domestic manufacturing for many PV system structural components, particularly for utility-scale systems. Some elements—such as torque tubes, piles, and select tracker assemblies—are widely produced domestically owing to their size and shipping constraints. Others, such as fasteners and certain rooftop components, still rely heavily on imports. Major steel components used in utility-scale PV systems represent only a small fraction of total U.S. steel consumption, which overall only has a 13% net import reliance. China is a major steel producer as well as a dominant manufacturer of finished steel PV products. Given China’s scale, low labor costs, and political strategy to export cheap goods, its products are often sold at a significant discount in global markets.
